description: We are a multidisciplinary team of students passionate about space, technology, healthcare, and innovation. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to explore how NASA’s open data can support astronaut health monitoring. We hope to develop a software-based solution that monitors key health indicators, identifies risks, and provides meaningful insights to support astronauts and mission teams.
summary:
Aither Kairos, developed by Team Astro Frontiers, is an astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support crew members during long-duration space missions. It brings together cardiovascular monitoring, cognitive health assessments, and internal jugular vein (IJV) ultrasound analysis in one platform.

Astronauts can enter their personal baseline measurements and compare future health indicators against those individual reference values. The platform includes ECG analysis, manual cardiovascular inputs, cognitive performance tracking, ultrasound analysis, health guidance, alerts, analysis history, and health reports.

By highlighting changes in health indicators, Aither Kairos aims to help astronauts better understand their health and support communication with ground medical teams. This is important because spaceflight conditions, including microgravity and isolation, can affect cardiovascular function and cognitive performance. Our goal is to contribute to safer, more informed health monitoring and support the future of long-duration space exploration.
details:
Aither Kairos — Project Details

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Aither Kairos, developed by Team Astro Frontiers, is a web-based astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support health awareness and decision-making during long-duration space missions. It combines cardiovascular monitoring, cognitive health assessment, and internal jugular vein (IJV) ultrasound analysis in one interface.

When an astronaut first logs in, they enter personal baseline health information. These measurements establish an individual reference profile. Future measurements can then be compared against that baseline to highlight changes rather than relying only on general population reference values.

The platform includes several key sections:

  • Health Overview: Displays heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), heart rate variability (HRV), cognitive readiness indicators, recent findings, and alerts.
  • Cardiovascular Health: Allows astronauts to upload ECG reports for ECG-FM-based analysis or manually enter cardiovascular measurements, including heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, HRV, and RMSSD. Results are compared with personal baseline values and presented through visual graphs.
  • Cognitive Health: Tracks processing speed through the Digit Symbol Substitution Test (DSST), working memory through 2-back accuracy, sustained attention through Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) reaction time, as well as fatigue and sleep duration.
  • IJV Monitoring: Provides an ultrasound upload and analysis workflow with a segmentation preview and cross-sectional area (CSA) estimation. The current prototype demonstrates this workflow using SegThy neck-ultrasound data.
  • Health Guidance: Presents informational guidance and possible next steps based on available analysis results.
  • Health Reports: Combines health information and analysis findings into reports that can support review by ground medical teams.
  • Analysis History and Settings: Keeps a record of previous analyses and allows users to update personal baseline information and account settings.

2. What benefits does it have?

Aither Kairos brings multiple health-monitoring functions together instead of requiring astronauts to consult separate tools for different health indicators. Its personal-baseline approach helps identify changes specific to each astronaut. Visual graphs, alerts, analysis history, and combined reports make health information easier to understand and review.

The platform also considers both physical and cognitive performance, recognizing that astronaut well-being involves more than cardiovascular measurements alone.

3. What is the intended impact?

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to conditions such as microgravity, radiation, isolation, and confinement. These conditions can affect cardiovascular function, blood circulation, cognitive performance, and overall well-being.

Our intended impact is to support astronauts in monitoring their health, recognizing potential changes earlier, and communicating useful information to medical teams on Earth. In the future, Aither Kairos could be expanded with real-time wearable integration, improved ultrasound analysis, and more advanced trend monitoring to support longer and more distant missions.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

Aither Kairos was developed as a web application using:

  • Frontend: TypeScript, HTML, and CSS.
  • Development environment: Visual Studio Code, Python virtual environments (venv).
  • Backend and analysis: Python-based processing for health-data and analysis workflows.
  • Machine learning: ECG-FM for the ECG analysis workflow.
  • Ultrasound demonstration: SegThy, a third-party neck-ultrasound segmentation dataset, used to demonstrate the IJV analysis workflow.
  • Data visualization: Graphs and dashboard components for displaying measurements and changes from personal baselines.

NASA's open research and data resources informed our understanding of spaceflight-related cardiovascular and cognitive health risks and helped guide the platform's features. Simulated values are used where real-time astronaut measurements are unavailable.

5. How is the project creative?

The main creative aspect of Aither Kairos is its focus on personalized health monitoring. Rather than simply comparing every astronaut against the same general reference ranges, it establishes individual baselines and uses them to highlight changes over time.

It also brings cardiovascular indicators, cognitive assessments, and IJV ultrasound analysis into a single platform. This integrated approach recognizes that physical health, circulation, and cognitive readiness are interconnected aspects of astronaut well-being.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered the unique challenges of monitoring health during long-duration missions, including limited access to immediate medical support, the importance of individual health differences, and the need for clear and accessible information.

We also considered data reliability, usability, and the limitations of a prototype. Some workflows demonstrate analysis using research or demonstration data and simulated values; they are not yet validated clinical diagnostic systems. Our design therefore focuses on supporting health awareness and medical review rather than replacing professional medical judgment.

Ultimately, Aither Kairos aims to contribute to a future where astronauts can monitor their health more effectively and explore farther with better health-support systems.
